title: the Mandukya Karika (Gaudapada)
hook: a coil on a dim path makes a walker's heart jump. a flashlight shows a rope. Gaudapada asks where the snake went

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Karika opened: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth, with Om laid over all of it. Did you catch the moment the waking room faded? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.
screen: `THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: THREE ROOMS AND A FOURTH.` · `A WEEK TO LOOK BACK ON.`

segments.voice: A man is coming home late, down a dim side path. Something lies coiled across the stones. A snake. His body reacts before he can think: a jump, a cold flush, a step back. Hands shaking, he finds his phone and turns on the light. It's a rope. Somebody dropped a length of rope. He laughs, a little too loud. And then, if he's the kind of person who wonders about things, a strange question arrives. Where did the snake go? It made his heart pound. It was real enough for that. Gaudapada asks this question in the Mandukya Karika, and his answer reaches back across our whole week.
screen: `A COIL ON THE PATH.` → `THE LIGHT: A ROPE.` → `WHERE DID THE SNAKE GO?`

segments.voice: First, the week. We spent six days with Shankara on the Brahma Sutra's first four lines, learning his word jnana, the knowing that undoes a mix-up. Yesterday we opened Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya, with its three states and the fourth. Today the two threads meet, because tradition places Gaudapada before Shankara, in Shankara's own lineage, and the mix-up gets a vivid picture in his verses. One section of the Karika is about how real the world we see is. He starts with dreams. Inside a dream, there are cities, roads, whole days of travel, and yet it all happens inside the sleeper. On waking, it's gone. Then he makes his bold move. What isn't there at the beginning and isn't there at the end, he says, isn't truly there in the middle either. Now the rope. A rope, not seen clearly in the dark, is imagined as a snake, or as a stream of water, or as other things. When the rope is seen for what it is, the imagining stops. In the same way, he says, the self is imagined as all kinds of things, and when the self is known, the imagining ends. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't say the snake turned into the rope, or crawled away. It was never anything apart from the rope. Gaudapada's reading is a hard one, and some other schools of Vedanta answer it: they hold the world to be real, the work of the Lord. Our week, read his way, ends with a flashlight on a path.
screen: `A WEEK OF JNANA, THEN THE MANDUKYA.` · `NOT AT THE START, NOT AT THE END.` · `THE ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.` · `THE SNAKE WAS NEVER APART FROM IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one fear in better light. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind one small worry that has been coiled on your path this week. Don't push it away. Just look at it, the way you'd shine a light on something in the dark. Ask, gently: what is actually here? Then let the question rest, and come back to the breath. If the worry stirs again, look once more, and return. If you pray, you can hold it up to the light you pray to. The bell holds the time.
The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, where a rope seen in the dark as a snake stands for the self taken for all kinds of things. Today's word.
Your line: the Mandukya Karika, Gaudapada. Today, when something startles you, take one breath and ask: rope or snake? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Advaita Vedanta teachers use the rope and the snake to explain how the world can be taken for something it isn't, and students reflect on the image in study and meditation.

fork.setup: the light shows a rope where you saw a snake. Gaudapada asks: where did the snake go? what's his answer?
options: it slithered off before the light came on.
it was never anything apart from the rope.
fork.reveal: when the rope is seen for what it is, the imagining simply stops. nothing went anywhere.

original.note: Sanskrit: a rope; in Gaudapada's image, the rope seen in the dark as a snake.

trapdoor: what you thought: the rope and snake just mean don't jump to conclusions.
what it means: in the Karika, the self is like the rope, and the many things it's taken for are like the snake.
what a scholar hears: Mandukya Karika 2.17–18, the rope imagined as snake or stream, in the section on unreality, vaitathya.

sources.ref: Mandukya Karika 2.1–2.6 (dream objects seen within the body; what is absent at the beginning and the end is so in the middle too)
Mandukya Karika 2.17–2.18 (a rope not clearly seen is imagined as a snake, a line of water and so on; when the rope is ascertained the imagining ceases; so with the self)
